papers.title: Let's Play Mono-Poly: BERT Can Reveal Words' Polysemy Level and\n Partitionability into Senses
papers.research_question: Do pre-trained language models encode knowledge about lexical polysemy and sense distinctions? Specifically, can BERT-derived representations reflect words' polysemy level and their partitionability into senses?
papers.core_contribution: BERT contextualized representations encode knowledge about words' polysemy level and their partitionability into senses, and this knowledge is present across multiple languages.
papers.conclusion: BERT representations reflect words' polysemy level and sense partitionability, opening new avenues for multilingual lexical semantics research and practical applications in WSD, lexicography, and cross-lingual transfer.
papers.key_findings:
BERT distinguishes monosemous from polysemous words across all layers and sentence pools, even when the polysemous words are presented in contexts of the same sense.
The self-similarity of a word's contextualized representations is inversely proportional to its polysemy level (higher polysemy leads to lower self-similarity).
BERT's ability to predict polysemy level is not solely reliant on word frequency or part of speech, as shown by controlled experiments.
BERT representations can indicate how easily a word's semantic space can be partitioned into distinct senses, as measured by clustering metrics.
The polysemy-related knowledge is more clearly present in English BERT, but monolingual models for French, Spanish, and Greek also show relevant distinctions, though with smaller effect sizes.
papers.limitation: The quality of automatic sense annotations in the Eurosense corpus varies across languages, which may affect the results for French, Spanish, and Greek.
future_direction: Extending the methodology to cross-lingual alignment and transfer, identifying polysemous words for which transfer is harder.
Applying the method to the study of lexical semantic change.
papers.abstract:
Pre-trained language models (LMs) encode rich information about linguistic
structure but their knowledge about lexical polysemy remains unclear. We
propose a novel experimental setup for analysing this knowledge in LMs
specifically trained for different languages (English, French, Spanish and
Greek) and in multilingual BERT. We perform our analysis on datasets carefully
designed to reflect different sense distributions, and control for parameters
that are highly correlated with polysemy such as frequency and grammatical
category. We demonstrate that BERT-derived representations reflect words'
polysemy level and their partitionability into senses. Polysemy-related
information is more clearly present in English BERT embeddings, but models in
other languages also manage to establish relevant distinctions between words at
different polysemy levels. Our results contribute to a better understanding of
the knowledge encoded in contextualised representations and open up new avenues
for multilingual lexical semantics research.

papers.title: Metaphors in Pre-Trained Language Models: Probing and Generalization Across Datasets and Languages
papers.research_question: Does pre-trained language models encode metaphorical knowledge, and how generalizable is this knowledge across languages and datasets?
papers.core_contribution: Pre-trained language models encode metaphorical knowledge, mostly in their middle layers, and this knowledge is transferable across languages and datasets when annotation is consistent.
papers.conclusion: Metaphorical knowledge exists in PLM representations, mainly in middle layers, and is transferable if annotation is consistent across training and testing data.
papers.key_findings:
PLMs encode metaphorical knowledge in their representations.
Metaphorical knowledge is concentrated in the middle layers of PLMs.
The knowledge is transferable across languages (cross-lingual generalization).
The knowledge is transferable across datasets but with larger gaps when annotations are inconsistent.
RoBERTa and ELECTRA encode metaphorical knowledge better than BERT.
papers.limitation: Due to resource limitations, experiments were conducted only on the base versions of models.
future_direction: Explore more the cross-lingual transfer of metaphors and the impact of cross-cultural similarities.
Apply metaphorical knowledge for text generation.
papers.abstract: Human languages are full of metaphorical expressions. Metaphors help people understand the world by connecting new concepts and domains to more familiar ones. Large pretrained language models (PLMs) are therefore assumed to encode metaphorical knowledge useful for NLP systems. In this paper, we investigate this hypothesis for PLMs, by probing metaphoricity information in their encodings, and by measuring the cross-lingual and crossdataset generalization of this information. We present studies in multiple metaphor detection datasets and in four languages (i.e., English, Spanish, Russian, and Farsi). Our extensive experiments suggest that contextual representations in PLMs do encode metaphorical knowledge, and mostly in their middle layers. The knowledge is transferable between languages and datasets, especially when the annotation is consistent across training and testing sets. Our findings give helpful insights for both cognitive and NLP scientists.

papers.title: Locating Language-Specific Information in Contextualized Embeddings
papers.research_question: How is language-specific information stored in multilingual pretrained language model representations, and can it be located in linear subspaces?
papers.core_contribution: This paper locates language-specific information in multilingual pretrained language models by projecting representations into linear subspaces using DensRay and LDA, showing that such information is scattered across dimensions and more prevalent in lower layers.
papers.conclusion: Language-specific information in multilingual representations can be decoded via linear subspaces, with dimensionality varying by task and lower layers being more language-specific, offering insights for improving cross-lingual transfer.
papers.key_findings:
Language-specific information is scattered across many dimensions and can be projected into a linear subspace.
The dimensionality of the language-specific subspace is task-dependent, with an upper bound roughly equal to the number of languages.
Lower layers of the models store more language-specific information compared to higher layers.
The proposed activity regularization method L-DAR can slightly improve zero-shot cross-lingual transfer performance in some cases.
For the NER task with multisource training, L-DAR does not consistently improve performance, indicating limitations.
papers.limitation: The activity regularization approach L-DAR leads to a performance drop on the NER task with multisource training, which is not fully understood and left for future research.
future_direction: Continuing research to better utilize language-specific information for improved zero-shot cross-lingual transfer performance.
papers.abstract: Multilingual pretrained language models (MPLMs) exhibit multilinguality and are well suited for transfer across languages. Most MPLMs are trained in an unsupervised fashion and the relationship between their objective and multilinguality is unclear. More specifically, the question whether MPLM representations are language-agnostic or they simply interleave well with learned task prediction heads arises. In this work, we locate language-specific information in MPLMs and identify its dimensionality and the layers where this information occurs. We show that language-specific information is scattered across many dimensions, which can be projected into a linear subspace. Our study contributes to a better understanding of MPLM representations, going beyond treating them as unanalyzable blobs of information.

papers.title: Unveiling LLMs: The Evolution of Latent Representations in a Dynamic Knowledge Graph
papers.research_question: Which factual knowledge do LLMs use to assess input truthfulness? How does this knowledge evolve across layers? Are there any distinctive patterns in its evolution?
papers.core_contribution: An end-to-end framework that decodes factual knowledge from LLM latent representations (as ground predicates) and represents its layer-wise evolution as a dynamic knowledge graph, enabling local and global interpretability analyses.
papers.conclusion: By decoding semantics from LLM latent representations and enabling graph-related analyses, this framework advances our understanding of the factual knowledge resolution process and the mechanistic interpretability of language models.
papers.key_findings:
Entity centrality is highlighted in LLM reasoning, from claim-related information and multi-hop reasoning to representation errors causing erroneous evaluations.
The global analysis reveals trends in the underlying evolution, such as word-based knowledge evolving into claim-related facts.
Early layers focus on syntax and entity resolution, while middle layers are crucial for factual knowledge resolution.
The framework can identify representation errors, such as entity confusion, duplication, and example leakage, that lead to incorrect evaluations.
The model's classification performance shows an imbalance, with higher precision for true claims and higher recall for false claims on FEVER, and more balanced recall on CLIMATE-FEVER.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) demonstrate an impressive capacity to recall a vast range of factual knowledge. However, understanding their underlying reasoning and internal mechanisms in exploiting this knowledge remains a key research area. This work unveils the factual information an LLM represents internally for sentence-level claim verification. We propose an end-to-end framework to decode factual knowledge embedded in token representations from a vector space to a set of ground predicates, showing its layer-wise evolution using a dynamic knowledge graph. Our framework employs activation patching, a vector-level technique that alters a token representation during inference, to extract encoded knowledge. Accordingly, we neither rely on training nor external models. Using factual and common-sense claims from two claim verification datasets, we showcase interpretability analyses at local and global levels. The local analysis highlights entity centrality in LLM reasoning, from claim-related information and multi-hop reasoning to representation errors causing erroneous evaluation. On the other hand, the global reveals trends in the underlying evolution, such as word-based knowledge evolving into claim-related facts. By interpreting semantics from LLM latent representations and enabling graph-related analyses, this work enhances the understanding of the factual knowledge resolution process.

papers.title: Joint processing of linguistic properties in brains and language models
papers.research_question: What linguistic properties are responsible for the alignment between brain recordings (fMRI) and language model representations?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a direct approach to evaluate joint linguistic processing in brains and language models by removing specific linguistic properties from model representations, showing this significantly decreases brain alignment, with syntactic properties having the largest effect.
papers.conclusion: The direct approach provides clear evidence that specific linguistic information, particularly syntactic properties, underlies the alignment between brain and language models, opening new avenues for mapping joint information processing.
papers.key_findings:
Removing each tested linguistic property (surface, syntactic, semantic) results in a significant decrease in brain alignment across all layers of BERT and GPT-2.
Syntactic properties (Top Constituents and Tree Depth) have the largest effect on the trend of brain alignment across model layers.
Top Constituents affects alignment in all language brain regions, while Tree Depth specifically affects temporal (ATL, PTL) and frontal (IFG, MFG) regions.
Semantic properties (Tense, Subject Number, Object Number) affect alignment more specifically in regions like the posterior cingulate cortex (PCC).
The method reveals that different linguistic properties are important for alignment in different brain regions and sub-regions.
papers.limitation:
The removal approach may also remove information correlated with the removed linguistic property due to dataset limitations.
Substantial brain alignment remains after removing all tested properties, indicating not all relevant linguistic properties have been accounted for.
The study is limited to English language stimuli and two language models (BERT and GPT-2).
future_direction: Incorporate additional linguistic properties to fully characterize joint processing.
Investigate larger language models beyond BERT and GPT-2.
Extend the approach to languages beyond English.
papers.abstract: Language models have been shown to be very effective in predicting brain recordings of subjects experiencing complex language stimuli. For a deeper understanding of this alignment, it is important to understand the correspondence between the detailed processing of linguistic information by the human brain versus language models. We investigate this correspondence via a direct approach, in which we eliminate information related to specific linguistic properties in the language model representations and observe how this intervention affects the alignment with fMRI brain recordings obtained while participants listened to a story. We investigate a range of linguistic properties (surface, syntactic, and semantic) and find that the elimination of each one results in a significant decrease in brain alignment. Specifically, we find that syntactic properties (i.e. Top Constituents and Tree Depth) have the largest effect on the trend of brain alignment across model layers. These findings provide clear evidence for the role of specific linguistic information in the alignment between brain and language models, and open new avenues for mapping the joint information processing in both systems. We make the code publicly available [https://github.com/subbareddy248/linguistic-properties-brain-alignment].

papers.title: How Does Unfaithful Reasoning Emerge from Autoregressive Training? A Study of Synthetic Experiments
papers.research_question: What constitutes faithful chain-of-thought reasoning and how does unfaithfulness emerge from autoregressive training?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a synthetic task (AER) to study chain-of-thought faithfulness, finds a critical noise threshold for faithful reasoning due to simplicity bias, and identifies training phases with emergent self-verification.
papers.conclusion: The study shows that unfaithful reasoning emerges when noise exceeds a critical threshold, driven by simplicity bias, and that models develop implicit self-verification through training dynamics.
papers.key_findings:
Faithful reasoning is possible only when training noise is below a critical threshold.
Simplicity bias explains the threshold: models prefer simpler stepwise reasoning over skip-step reasoning.
Training dynamics exhibit three reasoning modes: stepwise, mixed, skip-step, with a transient increase in prediction entropy in the mixed mode.
Models learn to encode internal uncertainty, suggesting emergent implicit self-verification.
Shortcut features amplify unfaithfulness.
papers.limitation:
Focus on autoregressive training, not reinforcement learning with verifier rewards.
Potential over-generalization of findings beyond the synthetic task.
future_direction: Investigate reinforcement learning with verifier rewards (RLVR).
Apply metrics to LLMs beyond synthetic setting.
papers.abstract: Chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning generated by large language models (LLMs) is often unfaithful: intermediate steps can be logically inconsistent or fail to reflect the causal relationship leading to the final answer. Despite extensive empirical observations, a fundamental understanding of CoT is lacking--what constitutes faithful CoT reasoning, and how unfaithfulness emerges from autoregressive training. We study these questions using well-controlled synthetic experiments, training small transformers on noisy data to solve modular arithmetic expressions step by step, a task we term Arithmetic Expression Reasoning. We find that models can learn faithful reasoning that causally follows the underlying arithmetic rules, but only when the training noise is below a critical threshold, a phenomenon attributable to simplicity bias. At higher noise levels, training dynamics exhibit a transition from faithful stepwise reasoning to unfaithful skip-step reasoning via an intermediate mixed mode characterized by a transient increase in prediction entropy. Mechanistic analysis reveals that models learn to encode internal uncertainty by resolving inconsistent reasoning steps, which suggests the emergence of implicit self-verification from autoregressive training.

papers.title: A Representation Level Analysis of NMT Model Robustness to Grammatical Errors
papers.research_question: How do NMT models represent and handle grammatical errors to achieve robustness? How does grammatical error representation differ across models and languages? How does fine-tuning for robustness influence models to achieve improved robustness?
papers.core_contribution: NMT encoders implement a grammatical error correction setup: they first detect grammatical errors and then correct them by moving the representation of the ungrammatical word toward its correct form. Fine-tuning for robustness increases reliance on Robustness Heads, which attend to interpretable linguistic units.
papers.conclusion: The encoder, especially after fine-tuning, implements a grammatical error correction setup by detecting and then correcting errors. Fine-tuning on grammatical errors leads the model to use more Robustness Heads, particularly in deeper layers.
papers.key_findings:
The encoder first detects grammatical errors (shown by GED probing) and then corrects them by moving the representation towards the correct form (shown by decreasing CKA distance).
Fine-tuned models rely more on Robustness Heads, especially in deeper layers, to update the ungrammatical word representation.
Models respond similarly to grammatical errors across architectures, but there are differences across languages due to linguistic features.
Fine-tuning only the encoder on noisy data is sufficient for improving robustness without degrading clean performance.
Robustness Heads attend to specific POS tags relevant to the error type (e.g., adjectives and nouns for article errors).
papers.limitation:
The analysis is limited to Indo-European languages, which may limit generalization to other languages.
Synthetic noise may not perfectly simulate natural noise.
The study focuses on relatively small models; larger models might behave differently.
future_direction: Extend the analysis to decoder-only models.
Analyze the effects of different pre-training strategies and training data on robustness.
papers.abstract: Understanding robustness is essential for building reliable NLP systems. Unfortunately, in the context of machine translation, previous work mainly focused on documenting robustness failures or improving robustness. In contrast, we study robustness from a model representation perspective by looking at internal model representations of ungrammatical inputs and how they evolve through model layers. For this purpose, we perform Grammatical Error Detection (GED) probing and representational similarity analysis. Our findings indicate that the encoder first detects the grammatical error, then corrects it by moving its representation toward the correct form. To understand what contributes to this process, we turn to the attention mechanism where we identify what we term *Robustness Heads*. We find that *Robustness Heads* attend to interpretable linguistic units when responding to grammatical errors, and that when we fine-tune models for robustness, they tend to rely more on *Robustness Heads* for updating the ungrammatical word representation.

papers.title: Counterfactual Interventions Reveal the Causal Effect of Relative Clause\n Representations on Agreement Prediction
papers.research_question: When language models process syntactically complex sentences, do they use their representations of syntax in a manner that is consistent with the grammar of the language?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces AlterRep, a counterfactual intervention method to test if language models use linguistic features consistently with grammar, and finds that BERT uses relative clause boundary information grammatically and abstractly.
papers.conclusion: AlterRep provides a way to test causal use of linguistic features in models, and shows BERT uses relative clause boundaries grammatically and abstractly.
papers.key_findings:
Only middle layers of BERT causally influence agreement prediction in a manner consistent with English grammar, while all layers encode RC boundary information.
RC boundary representations partially generalize across different RC types, suggesting abstract representation.
Interventions using random subspaces do not yield interpretable changes, indicating specificity of RC subspaces.
Similar patterns observed in BERT variants of different sizes, except BERT-tiny.
papers.limitation: AlterRep uses linear subspaces to analyze non-linear networks, so negative results may not be conclusive.
future_direction: Apply AlterRep to test hypotheses about a wide range of linguistic structures and tasks.
papers.abstract:
When language models process syntactically complex sentences, do they use
their representations of syntax in a manner that is consistent with the grammar
of the language? We propose AlterRep, an intervention-based method to address
this question. For any linguistic feature of a given sentence, AlterRep
generates counterfactual representations by altering how the feature is
encoded, while leaving intact all other aspects of the original representation.
By measuring the change in a model's word prediction behavior when these
counterfactual representations are substituted for the original ones, we can
draw conclusions about the causal effect of the linguistic feature in question
on the model's behavior. We apply this method to study how BERT models of
different sizes process relative clauses (RCs). We find that BERT variants use
RC boundary information during word prediction in a manner that is consistent
with the rules of English grammar; this RC boundary information generalizes to
a considerable extent across different RC types, suggesting that BERT
represents RCs as an abstract linguistic category.

papers.title: Finding Structure in Language Models
papers.research_question: Do language models possess a deep understanding of grammatical structure similar to humans, and how can such structures be identified?
papers.core_contribution: This dissertation demonstrates that language models capture abstract linguistic structure similar to humans, and develops interpretability techniques to reveal this structure. It shows that models exhibit structural priming, generalize from indirect evidence, and that interpretability methods must be evaluated with care.
papers.conclusion: The thesis provides a detailed account of grammatical knowledge in language models and offers directions for using computational methods to investigate linguistic questions.
papers.key_findings:
Language models exhibit human-like structural priming effects, indicating they capture abstract syntactic structure.
Language models can generalize linguistic patterns from indirect evidence, as shown by filtered corpus training experiments.
Interpretability methods for feature interaction detection vary in faithfulness and must be evaluated carefully.
Language models use monotonicity information to predict negative polarity item licensing.
Adjective order preferences in language models are influenced by data statistics and cognitive factors.
papers.abstract: When we speak, write or listen, we continuously make predictions based on our knowledge of a language's grammar. Remarkably, children acquire this grammatical knowledge within just a few years, enabling them to understand and generalise to novel constructions that have never been uttered before. Language models are powerful tools that create representations of language by incrementally predicting the next word in a sentence, and they have had a tremendous societal impact in recent years. The central research question of this thesis is whether these models possess a deep understanding of grammatical structure similar to that of humans. This question lies at the intersection of natural language processing, linguistics, and interpretability. To address it, we will develop novel interpretability techniques that enhance our understanding of the complex nature of large-scale language models. We approach our research question from three directions. First, we explore the presence of abstract linguistic information through structural priming, a key paradigm in psycholinguistics for uncovering grammatical structure in human language processing. Next, we examine various linguistic phenomena, such as adjective order and negative polarity items, and connect a model's comprehension of these phenomena to the data distribution on which it was trained. Finally, we introduce a controlled testbed for studying hierarchical structure in language models using various synthetic languages of increasing complexity and examine the role of feature interactions in modelling this structure. Our findings offer a detailed account of the grammatical knowledge embedded in language model representations and provide several directions for investigating fundamental linguistic questions using computational methods.

papers.title: ReflCtrl: Controlling LLM Reflection via Representation Engineering
papers.research_question: When does the model initiate reflection during its reasoning process? How does reflection influence the model's reasoning performance?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces ReflCtrl, a representation engineering framework that extracts a reflection direction in the latent space to control self-reflection in reasoning LLMs, and shows that reflections are often redundant and can be reduced to save inference cost without sacrificing performance.
papers.conclusion: The paper proposes ReflCtrl for controlling self-reflection in reasoning LLMs, demonstrates reflection redundancy and its connection to internal uncertainty, and shows that stepwise steering can reduce inference cost with minimal accuracy loss.
papers.key_findings:
Reflections are redundant, especially in stronger models, and up to 33.6% of reasoning tokens can be saved while preserving performance.
The model's reflection behavior is highly correlated with internal uncertainty signals, implying self-reflection may be controlled by model's uncertainty.
Stepwise steering can control reflection frequency and reduces performance loss compared to all-token steering.
The reflection direction can be used to predict answer correctness, suggesting it encodes uncertainty information.
Smaller models are more sensitive to reflection reduction than larger models.
papers.limitation:
Identification of reasoning steps relies on keyword search, which may be model specific.
ReflCtrl only works for open-source models and it remains unclear whether it generalizes to SOTA closed-source models such as GPT-4 or Claude.
future_direction: developing uncertainty-aware dynamic steering to adjust steering strength during inference
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) with Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning have achieved strong performance across diverse tasks, including mathematics, coding, and general reasoning. A distinctive ability of these reasoning models is self-reflection: the ability to review and revise previous reasoning steps. While self-reflection enhances reasoning performance, it also increases inference cost. In this work, we study self-reflection through the lens of representation engineering. We segment the model's reasoning into steps, identify the steps corresponding to reflection, and extract a reflection direction in the latent space that governs this behavior. Using this direction, we propose a stepwise steering method that can control reflection frequency. We call our framework ReflCtrl. Our experiments show that (1) in many cases reflections are redundant, especially in stronger models (in our experiments, we can save up to 33.6 percent of reasoning tokens while preserving performance), and (2) the model's reflection behavior is highly correlated with an internal uncertainty signal, implying self-reflection may be controlled by the model's uncertainty.

papers.title: Large Language Model probabilities cannot distinguish between possible and impossible language
papers.research_question: Does the grammaticality-ungrammaticality distinction have a unique surprisal signature in LLMs, such that we can infer ungrammaticality from minimal-pair surprisal differences?
papers.core_contribution: LLM probabilities cannot uniquely distinguish grammatical from ungrammatical sentences; surprisal is also affected by semantic and pragmatic violations, so probabilities are not reliable proxies for syntactic knowledge.
papers.conclusion: Probabilities are not reliable proxies for grammaticality, and claims about models distinguishing possible from impossible language need verification through a different methodology.
papers.key_findings:
Surprisal differences are significant for all violation conditions (ungrammatical, pragmatically odd, unsemantical) compared to the grammatical condition.
There is no unique surprisal signature for ungrammaticality; the unsemantical condition consistently shows higher surprisal than the ungrammatical condition.
Models are more surprised by semantic violations than syntactic violations.
Probabilities are too blunt a measure to establish a direct link to syntactic knowledge.
The hierarchy of impossible languages proposed by previous work is arbitrary and not theoretically justified.
papers.limitation:
The experiment only included the Reverse condition from Kallini et al.'s hierarchy, not the Shuffle condition.
The hierarchy of impossible languages lacks human comparisons and theoretical justification.
future_direction: Develop different testing methods to verify models' ability to distinguish possible from impossible language.
Conduct rigorous experiments with adequate comparisons to human baselines.
Develop better metrics for evaluating linguistic knowledge in LLMs.
papers.abstract: A controversial test for Large Language Models concerns the ability to discern possible from impossible language. While some evidence attests to the models' sensitivity to what crosses the limits of grammatically impossible language, this evidence has been contested on the grounds of the soundness of the testing material. We use model-internal representations to tap directly into the way Large Language Models represent the 'grammatical-ungrammatical' distinction. In a novel benchmark, we elicit probabilities from 4 models and compute minimal-pair surprisal differences, juxtaposing probabilities assigned to grammatical sentences to probabilities assigned to (i) lower frequency grammatical sentences, (ii) ungrammatical sentences, (iii) semantically odd sentences, and (iv) pragmatically odd sentences. The prediction is that if string-probabilities can function as proxies for the limits of grammar, the ungrammatical condition will stand out among the conditions that involve linguistic violations, showing a spike in the surprisal rates. Our results do not reveal a unique surprisal signature for ungrammatical prompts, as the semantically and pragmatically odd conditions consistently show higher surprisal. We thus demonstrate that probabilities do not constitute reliable proxies for model-internal representations of syntactic knowledge. Consequently, claims about models being able to distinguish possible from impossible language need verification through a different methodology.

papers.title: Just Say No to Single Embeddings: Why Your AI Needs Multiple Perspectives
papers.research_question: How does BERT represent linguistic features internally, and what is the geometric structure of these representations?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that BERT represents linguistic features in separate semantic and syntactic subspaces, provides evidence of fine-grained geometric representation of word senses, and gives a mathematical argument for the squared-distance tree embedding.
papers.conclusion: The paper's experiments suggest that BERT's internal geometry consists of multiple linear subspaces for different syntactic and semantic information, and that understanding this geometry can help improve transformer architectures.
papers.key_findings:
Attention matrices encode syntactic dependency relations, as shown by linear probes achieving high accuracy.
Parse tree embeddings in BERT approximate Pythagorean embeddings (squared Euclidean distance corresponds to tree distance), and there is a mathematical justification for this.
Word senses are represented as clusters in embedding space, and a simple nearest-neighbor classifier on BERT embeddings achieves state-of-the-art word sense disambiguation.
Semantic information can be isolated in a lower-dimensional subspace via a learned linear transformation (semantic probe).
Concatenating sentences with different word senses can cause embeddings to shift towards the opposing sense, indicating that tokens absorb meaning from all neighboring tokens.
future_direction: Investigating other meaningful subspaces in BERT's internal geometry
Using internal geometry to improve or refine transformer architectures
papers.abstract: Note: This is a work in progress document We present empirical evidence that conversations exhibit consistent geometric signatures when projected into different embedding spaces, alongside surprising variability in local feature detection. Analyzing 229 multi-agent AI dialogues from our prior study on social dynamics [Garcia, 2025], we examine whether geometric properties of conversational trajectories remain consistent across 5 fundamentally different embedding models. Our analysis reveals a striking dichotomy: while global geometric patterns (distance matrices, trajectory shapes) show remarkable consistency across both transformer-based and classical embeddings (correlations ranging from 0.521 to 0.957), local phase detection exhibits extreme variability (F1 scores from 0.08 to 0.36, agreement correlations from -0.14 to 0.76). This pattern of high global consistency with low local agreement suggests that different embedding models may capture distinct projections of conversations existing in a higher-dimensional semantic space. Transport-based analysis supports this interpretation, showing threefold increases in cross-paradigm distances compared to within-paradigm distances. These findings establish that while geometric analysis of conversation captures genuine structural properties, the global-local dichotomy implies fundamental limits on fine-grained analysis and raises intriguing questions about the true dimensionality of conversational dynamics.

papers.title: Extending a Mathematical Theory of the Emergence of Knowledge from the Experience to Capture Learning Dynamics in Transformers
papers.research_question: How do transformers' learning dynamics emerge from the structure of training data, and how does this relate to human semantic development?
papers.core_contribution: Extends a mathematical theory of learning dynamics to minimal transformers, demonstrating that learning trajectories are predictable from data structure and mirror human semantic development.
papers.conclusion: The work provides initial steps toward understanding how transformers learn, demonstrating that experience guides learning in a way that mirrors human semantic development, and the mathematical theory helps capture these dynamics.
papers.key_findings:
Learning occurs in two phases: fast reduction of loss-between via relation information, and slower reduction of loss-within via item information through attention.
Learning dynamics follow sigmoidal trajectories for dataset dimensions, as predicted by deep linear network theory.
The model exhibits progressive differentiation of concepts, learning broader categories before finer ones.
The model shows U-shaped learning for certain features, such as overgeneralization of properties.
Embeddings from the minimal transformer correlate with those from larger LLMs, suggesting relevance to scaled-up models.
papers.limitation: The study uses a simplified toy dataset and minimal transformer architecture, which may not fully capture complexities of natural language and larger models.
future_direction: Extending models and training sets to more natural language datasets.
Exploring how attentional strategies emerge for handling longer contextual dependencies.
papers.abstract: The Transformer architecture used in LLMs has garnered widespread attention due to these model's human-like conceptual knowledge and language understanding, yet understanding how these models' capabilities result from experience-guided learning, and connecting this learning process with the structure in their training data, can seem intractable. Here we present preliminary steps to characterizing the developmental trajectory of a minimal Transformer trained on a next-token prediction task, using a simple dataset with quantifiable uncertainty and a simple, intuitively characterizable structure that captures some aspects of natural semantic structure learned by LLMs from large datasets. We show how the dynamic learning process of this model is a predictable consequence of the structure of the training data, exhibiting attested features of human semantic development, as captured in a theory of neural network learning dynamics (Saxe et. al. 2019) previously used to capture such dynamics in a network originally introduced by Rumelhart & Todd (1993).

papers.title: Can LLMs Detect Their Confabulations? Estimating Reliability in Uncertainty-Aware Language Models
papers.research_question: How does in-context information influence model behavior and response uncertainty, and can uncertainty signals be used to predict response reliability?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a context-controlled evaluation framework to study how context quality affects LLM responses, shows that token-level uncertainty can misalign with correctness under misleading context, and proposes a probing-based method using uncertainty-guided hidden state aggregation for improved reliability detection.
papers.conclusion: Providing accurate context improves model accuracy and confidence, while misleading context leads to confidently incorrect outputs, revealing a misalignment between uncertainty and correctness. The probing-based approach using uncertainty-guided hidden state aggregation improves reliability detection over uncertainty-only baselines.
papers.key_findings:
Correct context improves both answer accuracy and model confidence.
Misleading context often induces confidently incorrect responses.
Token-level uncertainty does not always align with correctness, particularly under misleading context.
Probing classifiers using aggregated hidden states from high-uncertainty tokens outperform direct uncertainty metrics for reliability detection.
Aggregating features from multiple tokens yields better performance than single-token features.
future_direction: Developing reliability-aware generation and context validation/filtering mechanisms for multi-turn or retrieval-augmented generation.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are prone to generating fluent but incorrect content, known as confabulation, which poses increasing risks in multi-turn or agentic applications where outputs may be reused as context. In this work, we investigate how in-context information influences model behavior and whether LLMs can identify their unreliable responses. We propose a reliability estimation that leverages token-level uncertainty to guide the aggregation of internal model representations. Specifically, we compute aleatoric and epistemic uncertainty from output logits to identify salient tokens and aggregate their hidden states into compact representations for response-level reliability prediction. Through controlled experiments on open QA benchmarks, we find that correct in-context information improves both answer accuracy and model confidence, while misleading context often induces confidently incorrect responses, revealing a misalignment between uncertainty and correctness. Our probing-based method captures these shifts in model behavior and improves the detection of unreliable outputs across multiple open-source LLMs. These results underscore the limitations of direct uncertainty signals and highlight the potential of uncertainty-guided probing for reliability-aware generation.

papers.title: On the Similarity of Circuits across Languages: a Case Study on the Subject-verb Agreement Task
papers.research_question: How universal are the circuits implemented by language models for solving the same task across different languages? Specifically, the paper investigates whether the circuits for subject-verb agreement are similar in English and Spanish.
papers.core_contribution: The paper finds that the circuits for subject-verb agreement in English and Spanish in Gemma models are highly consistent, driven by an attention head that writes a language-independent subject number signal into the residual stream, which is read by downstream MLP neurons. This direction can causally steer the model's predictions across languages.
papers.conclusion: The circuits for subject-verb agreement are highly consistent across English and Spanish in Gemma models, with a language-independent subject number direction written by an attention head and read by MLP neurons, which can causally steer predictions across languages.
papers.key_findings:
The circuits for subject-verb agreement in English and Spanish are highly consistent in Gemma 2B.
A specific attention head (L13H7 in Gemma 2B) writes a subject number signal as a direction in the residual stream.
Downstream MLP neurons (e.g., neuron 2069 in MLP13) read this signal to promote the correct verb number.
The subject number direction is language-independent; steering with the English direction flips Spanish predictions.
Similar circuits are found in Gemma 7B and Gemma 2 2B, with analogous attention heads (L22H6 and L19H3) playing the same role.
papers.limitation:
The study focuses solely on Gemma models, which may not generalize to other model families.
The study is limited to two languages (English and Spanish), and cannot conclude that the same applies to all other languages, particularly those that are more linguistically distant.
future_direction: Further research could explore whether this pattern holds true for even larger models or across other model families.
papers.abstract: Several algorithms implemented by language models have recently been successfully reversed-engineered. However, these findings have been concentrated on specific tasks and models, leaving it unclear how universal circuits are across different settings. In this paper, we study the circuits implemented by Gemma 2B for solving the subject-verb agreement task across two different languages, English and Spanish. We discover that both circuits are highly consistent, being mainly driven by a particular attention head writing a `subject number' signal to the last residual stream, which is read by a small set of neurons in the final MLPs. Notably, this subject number signal is represented as a direction in the residual stream space, and is language-independent. We demonstrate that this direction has a causal effect on the model predictions, effectively flipping the Spanish predicted verb number by intervening with the direction found in English. Finally, we present evidence of similar behavior in other models within the Gemma 1 and Gemma 2 families.

papers.title: Latent Introspection: Models Can Detect Prior Concept Injections
papers.research_question: Can language models access information about their own prior internal states? Specifically, can they detect when concepts have been injected into their earlier context and identify which concept was injected?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that open-weight language models possess a latent capacity for introspection, enabling them to detect prior concept injections. This ability is often hidden in the residual stream and can be dramatically strengthened through specific prompting.
papers.conclusion: Language models have a surprising capacity for introspection and steering awareness that is easy to overlook, with consequences for latent reasoning and safety.
papers.key_findings:
Qwen2.5-Coder-32B-Instruct can detect prior concept injections, with detection signals emerging in middle layers (50–60) but attenuating in the final layers before output.
Prompting the model with accurate information about AI introspection mechanisms can increase detection sensitivity from 0.3% to 39.9% with only a 0.6% increase in false positives.
The model can identify which of nine concepts was injected earlier, with mutual information between injected and recovered concepts rising from 0.61 bits to 1.05 bits, ruling out generic noise explanations.
Detection capacity varies dramatically with prompting; a vague framing outperforms a mechanistically accurate description, achieving up to 84.0% accuracy.
The phenomenon generalizes to larger models (Llama 3.3 70B Instruct and Qwen 2.5 72B Instruct), though with different prompt sensitivities and signal strengths.
papers.limitation: The introspection signals are suppressed in the final layers of the model, which may be due to post-training effects (e.g., safety training), pretraining factors, or distribution shift.
future_direction: Distinguishing the causes of late-layer suppression (post-training vs. pretraining effects).
Mechanistic investigation of why vague framing outperforms accurate description in prompting.
papers.abstract: We uncover a latent capacity for introspection in a Qwen 32B model, demonstrating that the model can detect when concepts have been injected into its earlier context and identify which concept was injected. While the model denies injection in sampled outputs, logit lens analysis reveals clear detection signals in the residual stream, which are attenuated in the final layers. Furthermore, prompting the model with accurate information about AI introspection mechanisms can dramatically strengthen this effect: the sensitivity to injection increases massively (0.3% -> 39.2%) with only a 0.6% increase in false positives. Also, mutual information between nine injected and recovered concepts rises from 0.62 bits to 1.05 bits, ruling out generic noise explanations. Our results demonstrate models can have a surprising capacity for introspection and steering awareness that is easy to overlook, with consequences for latent reasoning and safety.

papers.title: A Philosophical Introduction to Language Models - Part II: The Way Forward
papers.research_question: What are the philosophical implications of recent progress in LLMs, particularly regarding interpretability, multimodality, consciousness, reproducibility, and their relevance to modeling human cognition?
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides a philosophical exploration of issues raised by LLMs, arguing for the importance of mechanistic interpretability through causal intervention methods and discussing the implications of multimodal extensions, consciousness debates, and reproducibility concerns.
papers.conclusion: LLM-like systems may be relevant to modeling aspects of human cognition if their architectural characteristics and learning scenarios are adequately constrained, but further research is needed to address interpretability and reproducibility challenges.
papers.key_findings:
Benchmarks for LLMs are limited by saturation, gamification, contamination, and construct validity issues, which undermine their reliability for assessing model capacities.
Causal intervention methods, such as ablation and activation editing, are necessary for achieving mechanistic understanding of LLMs' internal representations and computations.
Multimodal models often exhibit compositional failures due to their training objectives (e.g., contrastive learning) rather than inherent architectural limitations of the Transformer.
There are ongoing debates about whether LLMs could meet minimal criteria for consciousness, though current evidence is insufficient and the analogy to biological consciousness is problematic.
LLM research faces significant issues of secrecy and reproducibility, which hinder scientific progress and trust in reported capabilities.
future_direction: Advancing mechanistic interpretability through causal intervention methods to understand LLMs' internal mechanisms.
Addressing reproducibility and secrecy issues in LLM research to foster open scientific inquiry.
Exploring the potential of LLMs as models of human cognition by constraining their architecture and learning scenarios appropriately.
papers.abstract: In this paper, the second of two companion pieces, we explore novel philosophical questions raised by recent progress in large language models (LLMs) that go beyond the classical debates covered in the first part. We focus particularly on issues related to interpretability, examining evidence from causal intervention methods about the nature of LLMs' internal representations and computations. We also discuss the implications of multimodal and modular extensions of LLMs, recent debates about whether such systems may meet minimal criteria for consciousness, and concerns about secrecy and reproducibility in LLM research. Finally, we discuss whether LLM-like systems may be relevant to modeling aspects of human cognition, if their architectural characteristics and learning scenario are adequately constrained.

papers.title: Ecco: An Open Source Library for the Explainability of Transformer Language Models
papers.research_question: What is the level of syntactic information in BERT's FFNN representations compared to hidden states, and how does syntactic information evolve across layers?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Ecco, an open-source library for explainability of Transformer language models, and uses it to find that syntactic information in BERT's FFNN representations is comparable to hidden states, and that hidden states build up syntactic information even when intermediate FFNNs show diminished levels.
papers.conclusion: Ecco is a tool that aids in debugging, explaining, and building intuitions about Transformer language models, and it is open-source for community contribution.
papers.key_findings:
Syntactic information can be retrieved from BERT's FFNN representations at levels comparable to hidden state representations.
The model builds up syntactic information in its hidden states even when intermediate FFNNs indicate diminished levels of syntactic information.
Ecco provides tools for input saliency (gradient-based feature attribution), hidden state evolution analysis, and neuron activation analysis via dimensionality reduction and probing.
The library supports multiple explainability methods (e.g., CCA, NMF, probing) and models (GPT2, BERT, RoBERTa).
Ecco enables interactive exploration of model internals within Jupyter notebooks.
papers.limitation:
Ecco's input saliency feature is currently only supported for GPT2-based models, while neuron activation collection and dimensionality reduction are supported for GPT2, BERT, and RoBERTa.
Visualization is a starting point for building testable and falsifiable hypotheses of model interpretability, not a definitive explanation.
future_direction: Support for more models and explainability methods is under development and open for community contribution.
Future work can examine if the divergence in PoS information between FFNN and hidden states points towards layers storing different subsets of PoS information which the model assembles across layers.
papers.abstract: J Alammar. Proceedings of the 59th Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics and the 11th International Joint Conference on Natural Language Processing: System Demonstrations. 2021.

papers.title: Contributions of Transformer Attention Heads in Multi- and Cross-lingual Tasks
papers.research_question: What are the effects of pruning attention heads in multilingual Transformer-based models on cross-lingual and multi-lingual tasks, and how can important heads be identified?
papers.core_contribution: This paper shows that pruning a subset of attention heads in multilingual Transformer models (mBERT and XLM-R) generally improves performance in cross-lingual and multi-lingual sequence labeling tasks, and introduces a gradient-based method to rank and identify which heads to prune.
papers.conclusion: Pruning attention heads in multilingual Transformer models generally improves performance in cross-lingual and multi-lingual sequence labeling tasks, and the gradient-based method effectively identifies heads to prune, offering better model interpretability and efficiency.
papers.key_findings:
Pruning attention heads in mBERT and XLM-R generally has positive effects on model performance in cross-lingual and multi-lingual sequence labeling tasks (POS, NER, SF).
A gradient-based method can effectively rank attention heads by importance, and pruning the lowest-ranked heads leads to performance improvements.
The important attention heads for a task are shared across languages, as evidenced by high correlation in head rankings across different languages.
Pruning attention heads is beneficial even when training data in the target language is limited, making models more applicable to resource-poor languages.
In multi-source language settings, pruning attention heads also improves performance, and the gradient-based ranking method can be extended to multiple source languages.
papers.limitation: The study is limited to sequence labeling tasks (POS, NER, SF) and may not generalize to other cross-lingual tasks.
future_direction: Improving model interpretability in other cross-lingual and multi-lingual tasks, e.g., XNLI and other passage-level classification tasks.
papers.abstract: Weicheng Ma, Kai Zhang, Renze Lou, Lili Wang, Soroush Vosoughi. Proceedings of the 59th Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics and the 11th International Joint Conference on Natural Language Processing (Volume 1: Long Papers). 2021.

papers.title: Emotions Where Art Thou: Understanding and Characterizing the Emotional Latent Space of Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How do large language models (LLMs) internally represent emotion by analyzing the geometry of their hidden-state space?
papers.core_contribution: This work reveals a consistent and manipulable affective geometry in LLMs, showing that emotional representations form a low-dimensional, directionally encoded subspace that generalizes across datasets and languages, and can be steered via targeted interventions.
papers.conclusion: The findings reveal a consistent and manipulable affective geometry in LLMs and offer insight into how they internalize and process emotion.
papers.key_findings:
A low-dimensional emotional manifold exists in LLMs, with emotional representations being directionally encoded, distributed across layers, and aligned with interpretable dimensions.
The emotional structure is stable across depth and generalizes to eight real-world emotion datasets spanning five languages.
Cross-domain alignment yields low error and strong linear probe performance, indicating a universal emotional subspace.
Internal emotion perception can be steered while preserving semantics using a learned intervention module, with especially strong control for basic emotions across languages.
Emotional information is not localized but distributed broadly and redundantly throughout the network, with high separability emerging from overlapping, multi-purpose components.
papers.limitation: The steering technique does not uniformly override model behavior but respects representational limits, with variability in steerability across languages and domains (e.g., low-resource or archaic corpora) functioning as an inherent boundary.
papers.abstract: This work investigates how large language models (LLMs) internally represent emotion by analyzing the geometry of their hidden-state space. The paper identifies a low-dimensional emotional manifold and shows that emotional representations are directionally encoded, distributed across layers, and aligned with interpretable dimensions. These structures are stable across depth and generalize to eight real-world emotion datasets spanning five languages. Cross-domain alignment yields low error and strong linear probe performance, indicating a universal emotional subspace. Within this space, internal emotion perception can be steered while preserving semantics using a learned intervention module, with especially strong control for basic emotions across languages. These findings reveal a consistent and manipulable affective geometry in LLMs and offer insight into how they internalize and process emotion.

papers.title: Linguistically Grounded Analysis of Language Models using Shapley Head Values
papers.research_question: How is linguistic knowledge, specifically morphosyntactic phenomena, encoded and processed in language models?
papers.core_contribution: Shapley Head Value (SHV) attributions can identify subnetworks in language models that correspond to linguistic phenomena, supporting the hypothesis that models learn linguistically grounded internal structures.
papers.conclusion: SHV-based attributions can identify attention heads of subnetworks that generalize across related morphosyntactic phenomena, enabling linguistically grounded analysis of language models.
papers.key_findings:
Clusters of BLiMP paradigms based on SHVs show consistency across BERT and RoBERTa models.
Clusters often group paradigms from the same linguistic category, indicating models organize knowledge by linguistic phenomena.
Pruning analysis shows linguistic knowledge is often localized in specific attention heads.
RoBERTa is more discerning than BERT in separating linguistic phenomena, likely due to more pretraining data and parameters.
SHVs are useful for identifying subnetworks that generalize across related morphosyntactic phenomena.
papers.limitation:
Difficulty scaling to new languages and models due to lack of datasets and need for manual linguistic analysis.
BLiMP sentences are semantically empty and formulaic, though this is balanced between grammatical and ungrammatical examples.
SHV derivation uses sampling and heuristics, introducing uncertainty in attribution accuracy.
Binary gates for pruning may cause out-of-distribution issues, making it hard to disentangle head importance from ablation impact.
Attribution at the attention head level loses granularity compared to neuron-level analysis.
future_direction: Applying the methods to cross-lingual settings to describe subnetworks specific to linguistic knowledge in language models.
papers.abstract: Understanding how linguistic knowledge is encoded in language models is crucial for improving their generalisation capabilities. In this paper, we investigate the processing of morphosyntactic phenomena, by leveraging a recently proposed method for probing language models via Shapley Head Values (SHVs). Using the English language BLiMP dataset, we test our approach on two widely used models, BERT and RoBERTa, and compare how linguistic constructions such as anaphor agreement and filler-gap dependencies are handled. Through quantitative pruning and qualitative clustering analysis, we demonstrate that attention heads responsible for processing related linguistic phenomena cluster together. Our results show that SHV-based attributions reveal distinct patterns across both models, providing insights into how language models organize and process linguistic information. These findings support the hypothesis that language models learn subnetworks corresponding to linguistic theory, with potential implications for cross-linguistic model analysis and interpretability in Natural Language Processing (NLP).

papers.title: I Spy With My Model's Eye: Visual Search as a Behavioural Test for MLLMs
papers.research_question: Does the visual processing of multimodal large language models exhibit human-like pop-out effects and capacity limits in visual search tasks?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces visual search paradigms as a cognitively grounded diagnostic tool for evaluating perceptual capabilities in MLLMs, finding that advanced models exhibit human-like pop-out effects and capacity limits in conjunctive search.
papers.conclusion: Visual search tasks provide a valuable behavioural test for understanding MLLM perceptual capabilities and can serve as a cognitively grounded diagnostic tool.
papers.key_findings:
GPT-4o exhibits human-like pop-out effects in disjunctive search tasks (e.g., large target among smaller ones) with set-size independent accuracy.
MLLMs show capacity limits in conjunctive search tasks, with accuracy declining as distractor set size increases.
Some MLLMs incorporate natural scene priors, such as a bias for vertical lighting gradients and better detection of bottom-lit spheres.
Fine-tuning on conjunctive search tasks improves performance and generalizes to out-of-distribution set sizes and similar shape tasks.
Mechanistic interpretability reveals that disjunctive search tasks are resolved in earlier layers, while conjunctive tasks require deeper layers.
papers.limitation: Fine-tuning on conjunctive search tasks improves performance but does not reach pop-out levels.
papers.abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) achieve strong performance on vision-language tasks, yet their visual processing is opaque. Most black-box evaluations measure task accuracy, but reveal little about underlying mechanisms. Drawing on cognitive psychology, we adapt classic visual search paradigms -- originally developed to study human perception -- to test whether MLLMs exhibit the ``pop-out'' effect, where salient visual features are detected independently of distractor set size. Using controlled experiments targeting colour, size and lighting features, we find that advanced MLLMs exhibit human-like pop-out effects in colour or size-based disjunctive (single feature) search, as well as capacity limits for conjunctive (multiple feature) search. We also find evidence to suggest that MLLMs, like humans, incorporate natural scene priors such as lighting direction into object representations. We reinforce our findings using targeted fine-tuning and mechanistic interpretability analyses. Our work shows how visual search can serve as a cognitively grounded diagnostic tool for evaluating perceptual capabilities in MLLMs.

papers.title: Large Language Models as Neurolinguistic Subjects: Discrepancy between Performance and Competence
papers.research_question: What is the distinction between performance and competence in LLMs' linguistic understanding? How do LLMs represent form and meaning across languages?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a neurolinguistic method (minimal pair probing) to assess LLMs' linguistic competence, revealing a distinction between performance and competence, and showing LLMs have stronger form competence than meaning competence.
papers.conclusion: This study adopts both psycho- and neuro-linguistic approaches to evaluating LLMs, revealing a distinction between linguistic performance and competence, and highlights the limitations of LLMs' semantic understanding.
papers.key_findings:
Psycholinguistic and neurolinguistic methods reveal that language performance and competence are distinct.
Direct probability measurement may not accurately assess linguistic competence.
Instruction tuning improves performance but does not significantly change competence.
LLMs exhibit higher competence and performance in form compared to meaning.
LLMs encode form earlier than meaning.
papers.limitation:
Limited range of languages covered in experiments.
Poor German evaluation results potentially due to very long sentences in the DistilLingEval dataset.
Experiments conducted on small-scale LLMs due to computational resource constraints.
COMPS dataset for conceptual understanding is not sufficiently fine-grained, limited to only four types of conceptual relationships.
future_direction: Include experiments covering a wider range of languages.
Construct syntactic minimal pair datasets for German.
Explore larger models to validate and extend generalizability.
papers.abstract: This study investigates the linguistic understanding of Large Language Models (LLMs) regarding signifier (form) and signified (meaning) by distinguishing two LLM assessment paradigms: psycholinguistic and neurolinguistic. Traditional psycholinguistic evaluations often reflect statistical rules that may not accurately represent LLMs' true linguistic competence. We introduce a neurolinguistic approach, utilizing a novel method that combines minimal pair and diagnostic probing to analyze activation patterns across model layers. This method allows for a detailed examination of how LLMs represent form and meaning, and whether these representations are consistent across languages. We found: (1) Psycholinguistic and neurolinguistic methods reveal that language performance and competence are distinct; (2) Direct probability measurement may not accurately assess linguistic competence; (3) Instruction tuning won't change much competence but improve performance; (4) LLMs exhibit higher competence and performance in form compared to meaning. Additionally, we introduce new conceptual minimal pair datasets for Chinese (COMPS-ZH) and German (COMPS-DE), complementing existing English datasets.

papers.title: Semantic maps and the identification of cross-linguistic generic categories: evidentiality and its relation to epistemic modality
papers.abstract: The article, Semantic maps and the identification of cross-linguistic generic categories: evidentiality and its relation to epistemic modality, in the journal, Linguistic Discovery, Volume 8, Issue 1, Year 2010

papers.title: Evidentiality, Modality, and Speech Acts
papers.abstract: Evidential constructions have two main semantic effects: They contribute information about an individual's source of evidence, and they potentially modify the force of a sentence. In this article, I review the at-issue status of the evidential information, the indexical and anaphoric properties of evidentials, their force-modifying effect, and the connection throughout to epistemic modality. In some languages, evidentials occur as part of the grammatical morphology, but evidential information can be expressed through a variety of constructions across languages. As such, the study of evidentiality highlights the important role of cross-linguistic semantics and the collaboration between language typology and linguistic semantics.

papers.title: Evidentiality and Epistemic Modality
papers.abstract: Evidentiality and Epistemic Modality: Conceptual and Descriptive Issues presents ground-breaking research on the domains of evidentiality and epistemic modality. The book includes papers on key theoretical issues (the nature of evidential inference and the challengeability criterion for evidentiality), and descriptive studies covering various European languages (English, Spanish, French, German, Dutch, Italian, Romanian, Catalan and Latvian), based on general corpora or specific discourse types. The prominent corpus-based contrastive methodology uncovers a wide range of idiosyncratic discourse-pragmatic features of diverse languages, discourses and genres. The contributions are representative of the work on evidentiality and epistemic modality in a substantial number of countries.

papers.title: Typological variation in the expression of Evidentiality
papers.abstract: This article examines evidentiality as a complex and debated concept in linguistics. While scholars disagree on whether evidentiality is a grammatical or lexical category, there is consensus that its core function is to indicate the source of information. It answers epistemological questions such as: Was the event directly witnessed? Was it inferred from evidence? Was it learned through hearsay or reports? The article analyzes how evidentiality is expressed in Azerbaijani, English, and Spanish, focusing on both grammatical and lexical strategies. By comparing these languages, the study reveals typological differences and highlights the role of evidentiality in communication. It also discusses the relationship between evidentiality and epistemic modality, showing how both influence the speaker’s stance and interpretation of truth.

papers.title: Evidentiality In Romance Languages. Explanatory Potential of a Concept and Its Applications In Pragmatics
papers.abstract: Defined narrowly, evidentiality pertains to the sources of knowledge or evidence whereby the speaker feels entitled to make a factual claim. But evidentiality may also be conceived more broadly as both providing epistemic justification and reflecting speaker’s attitude towards the validity of the communicated information, and hearer’s potential acceptability of the information, derived from the degree of reliability of the source and mode of access to the information. Evidentiality and epistemic modality are subcategories of the same superordinate category, namely a category of epistemicity. Since the first seminal works on evidentiality (Chafe and Nichols 1986), studies have for the most part centred on languages where the grammatical marking of the information source is obligatory (for example Willett 1988; Aikhenvald 2004). Recent years have witnessed a growing interest in the study of the domain of evidentiality in European languages, which rely on strategies along the lexico‐grammatical continuum. Assuming a broad conception of evidentiality and defining it as a functional category, we study linguistic means that fulfil the function of indicating the source of information for the transmitted content of a certain proposition in Romance languages.

papers.title: The links between evidentiality, modality, and grammaticalization
papers.abstract: Abstract This paper introduces the main notions that are addressed in this special issue, namely evidentiality, modality, and grammaticalization. It defines each notion and briefly synthesizes the literature. It also presents some of the controversies which surround the ideas that prevail in these research fields. Crosslinguistic examples illustrate the main evidential and modal categories, and clarify why the two domains are both distinct and related. The paper then sketches the main pathways of grammaticalization of modal and evidential markers as they have been documented in typological work. Finally, it introduces the contributions to this special issue, highlights the new insights, and discusses what remains to be investigated on the links between evidentiality, modality, and grammaticalization.

papers.title: Evidentiality, epistemic modality and temporality in the Spanish verbal system
papers.abstract: In the current literature on TAM categories in European languages, and more specifically in Spanish, the notion of evidentiality has been introduced as a potential new category, more or less linked to modality, in the study of the verbal system. In this paper we challenge the non-modal dimension of evidentiality in Spanish as it appears in the description of some verb forms such as the Future, the Conditional and the Indicative Imperfect. We argue that most of these “evidential” uses can be explained in terms of the traditional categories of tense and epistemic modality with the help of well-established notions in the description of the Spanish verb, such as inactuality, polifunctionality and semantic displacement. We also deal with the study of two compound forms of the Indicative − the Past Perfect and the Present Perfect − which in some American varieties are used in non-standard ways that may coincide with evidential functions. In any case, we recommend a critical approach to all such phenomena based on broader and contextualised data before ruling out their integration into the TAM categories, as described hitherto.

papers.title: Evidentiality and epistemic modality in the semantics of the German verbs sollen and wollen (based on the data from the German-Russian parallel corpus)
papers.abstract: Based on the analysis of the semantics of the German modal verbs sollen and wollen and their translational equivalents identified in the German-Russian parallel subcorpus of the Russian National Corpus (RNC), the article demonstrates that the categories of evidentiality and epistemic modality should be considered as having an independent status. At the same time, these two linguistic meanings can be expressed simultaneously. We consider possible combinations of the types of evidential and epistemic meaning components expressed by these German verbs. We clarify the classification of indirect evidentiality types by introducing the third intermediate type – reportative-inferential evidentiality, i.e. a conclusion made by the speaker based on the interpretation of someone else’s utterance. Addressing the parallel corpus made it possible, on the one hand, to distinguish between the types of evidential meanings expressed by the verbs sollen and wollen, on the other hand, to clarify the semantics and identify the potential polysemy of the Russian translation equivalents.

papers.title: Evidentiality
papers.abstract: Human societies show a deep concern with how people know things and how relationships to knowledge are constructed and portrayed in talk. The term evidentiality refers to particular linguistic resources for talking about knowledge and especially to grammaticalized markers that indicate knowledge sources. Evidential marking is found in diverse languages around the world. This review discusses cross-linguistic evidential meanings and examines research on evidentials in practice, with a focus on their interpretation as stance markers and deictic elements. Evidentiality is a fascinating accomplishment in language structure, meaning, and use and can tell us about shared and disparate visions of knowledge and sociality across cultures.

papers.title: Evidentiality and epistemic modality: Overlap view within word semantics
papers.abstract: The starting point for this paper was the profound works by S. T. Nefedov who analyzed a wide range of problems in the field of modality. The article studies the specificity of the relationship between the two categories of epistemic modality and evidentiality. The former is used by the speaker to provide a source or evidence for the speaker’s claim, the latter performatively expresses the subjective opinion about the truth of a proposition. Despite the independent status recognized for evidentiality and epistemic modality, they are realized within the same proposition. The study of their relation is approached in this paper through the prototypical evidential marker hearsay. The choice of the marker is caused by its complex semantics combining epistemic and evidential components that allows to clarify the nature of the relations between the categories under study. The semasiological and onomasiological approaches to achieve the goal are realized by means of componential analysis supplemented with a number of techniques of the logical-semantic conception, as well as the contextual method. The analysis and generalization of the lexicographic meaning of the word hearsay revealed five lexico-semantic variants within the semanteme. At the level of the semantics of the evidential, the epistemic meaning is incorporated into the componential composition of all the sememes. The paper introduces the term “interplay” to denote the ambiguous and asymmetric nature of the evidentiality and epistemic modality integration. In addition, their interplay turns out to be inferent. This is expressed in the difference in distance from the source of acquired knowledge (second/ third-hand evidence attributed to the quotative and the reportative respectively) conveyed in the semanteme that implies a different degree of epistemicity manifesting gradient properties. Thus, an appeal to the notion of evidence and a level approach to its classification contributes to a deeper understanding of the reasons for the expansion of evidential meanings and the nature of their overlap with epistemic ones.

papers.title: Relations Between Language and Cognition: Evidentiality and Sources of Knowledge
papers.abstract: Understanding and acquiring language involve mapping language onto conceptual representations. Nevertheless, several issues remain unresolved with respect to (a) how such mappings are performed, and (b) whether conceptual representations are susceptible to cross-linguistic influences. In this article, we discuss these issues focusing on the domain of evidentiality and sources of knowledge. Empirical evidence in this domain yields growing support for the proposal that linguistic categories of evidentiality are tightly linked to, build on, and reflect conceptual representations of sources of knowledge that are shared across speakers of different languages.

papers.title: Evidentiality in English and Polish
papers.abstract: This thesis provides a synchronic account of evidentiality in English and Polish and the main ideas associated with the research on evidentiality with reference to these languages. Chapter 1 provides the review of main ideas as presented in the literature on the topic. Linguists provide varied definitions of evidentiality, therefore chapter 2 gives a unified description of evidentiality, understood as an independent grammatical and semantic category, and offers an organised account of its semantic types and sub-types. Chapter 3 and 4 analyse evidentiality in English and Polish, respectively, describing various lexical items with evidential meaning. Chapter 5 addresses the issue of the relation between evidentiality and other grammatical categories, while the final chapter looks at the correlation between evidentiality and epistemic modality.

papers.title: Evidentiality, Epistemic Modality and Mirativity: The Case of Cantonese Utterance Particles Ge3, Laak3, and Lo1
papers.abstract: This thesis examines a set of three utterance particles—ge3, laak3, and lo1—in Hong Kong Cantonese in terms of evidentiality, epistemic modality, and mirativity. Cantonese utterance particles have long been studied; however, close investigation of evidentiality and mirativity on a small set of particles is relatively rare. Previous accounts claim that ge3 and laak3 convey certainty. On the other hand, linguists also claim that the use of the utterance particle lo1 assumes a high level of knowledge from a hearer.
